documents.abstract: The Indian banking industry is undergoing a paradigm shift driven by rapid technological advancements, digital transformation, and evolving customer expectations. Artificial Intelligence (AI), as a subset of advanced digital technologies, has emerged as a transformative force capable of redefining banking operations across all segments of the financial system. Scheduled Public Sector Banks, Private Sector Banks, and Cooperative Banks are increasingly adopting AI-based applications to improve operational efficiency, customer service, credit appraisal, fraud detection, cybersecurity, human resource management, and marketing effectiveness. AI enables banks to analyze large volumes of structured and unstructured data in real time, automate repetitive processes, predict customer behavior, and enhance decision-making with greater accuracy and speed.Over the last five financial years (FY 2020–FY 2025), the Indian banking sector has demonstrated significant improvement in financial health. Gross Non-Performing Assets (GNPAs) have declined to multi-year lows, while profitability has reached record levels due to strengthened risk management, improved governance, digital banking initiatives, and regulatory reforms introduced by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and the Government of India. AI has played an increasingly important role by enabling predictive analytics for credit risk assessment, early warning systems for loan defaults, automated compliance monitoring, personalized customer engagement, and intelligent cybersecurity mechanisms.This research paper examines the effectiveness of AI adoption across different categories of Indian banks, with special emphasis on its impact on human resource utilization, reduction of NPAs, profitability enhancement, marketing strategies, fraud prevention, and cybersecurity resilience. The study adopts a descriptive and analytical research design based on secondary data collected from RBI publications, Government reports, annual reports of major banks, and academic literature. Comparative analysis is undertaken using financial indicators from leading Public Sector Banks, Private Sector Banks, and Cooperative Banks during the period 2020–2025.The study concludes that AI has significantly improved operational efficiency, customer satisfaction, and financial performance in the Indian banking industry. However, challenges relating to data privacy, ethical AI, infrastructure costs, shortage of skilled manpower, algorithmic transparency, and regulatory compliance continue to constrain widespread adoption, particularly among Cooperative Banks. The paper recommends the development of a comprehensive national AI strategy for banking, enhanced investment in digital infrastructure, employee upskilling, standardized AI governance frameworks, and collaborative initiatives between regulators, banks, fintech firms, and academic institutions.

Despite increasing efforts of legislatures to prohibit specialized AI-driven apps from providing therapeutic decision-making, general-purpose Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being used as alternative tools for mental health support. In this paper, we examine the increased adoption of AI for mental health through the lens of proponents’ and opponents’ discussions on public forums. Through a qualitative analysis of 67 Reddit discussion threads (totaling 2948 comments), we offer an in-depth investigation of the various contexts in which users rely on (or fail to rely on) AI for mental health support, as well as an analysis of the main discussions (including positions for and against the use of AI for therapy) within the community. By critically reflecting on our findings, we highlight ethical considerations and discuss how research, design and regulation of AI tools can help improve mental health support for users with complicated needs while mitigating potential harms.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study examines how artificial intelligence (AI) innovation influences corporate energy efficiency and the underlying mechanisms. We develop a general equilibrium model incorporating energy input and endogenous AI technology to explain how AI innovation improves energy efficiency through production process optimization. Using a deep-learning-based text identification, we develop a firm-level measure of AI innovation for Chinese listed companies over the period 2008–2022. Our empirical results show that AI innovation significantly improves corporate energy efficiency, while the mechanism analysis provides evidence consistent with production process optimization as an important transmission channel. This positive effect is stronger among firms operating in key technological sectors and capital-intensive industries. Further, we find that disruptive AI innovation produces a larger effect than general AI innovation. We also document that local governments' attention to AI development and intra-firm data sharing strengthen the energy-efficiency gains associated with AI innovation. This study contributes to research on digital innovation and firm sustainability by showing how AI-driven innovation translates into efficiency-enhancing outcomes through organizational and data-governance mechanisms.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Aim and Objectives-The primary aim of this study was to evaluate the efficacy of Conventional local anesthesia delivery system and computer controlled local anesthetic drug delivery system.Specific objectives included assessing pain levels, onset of anesthesia, patient comfort, and anxiety levels, as well as monitoring hemodynamic changes (Blood Pressure and SpO2) during and after deposition of local anesthesia.Material and Methods-In this study 50 patients were divided into 2 equal group.Group A received local anesthesia via CCLAD system, while Group B received local anesthesia from traditional manual syringe.Results-The intergroup comparison of comfort levels between the Study and Control groups showed a statistically significant difference (χ² = 15.263,p = 0.003).In the Study Group, 24% of subjects were very comfortable and 36% were comfortable, while 40% reported only mild discomfort.No participant in the Study Group reported uncomfortable or extremely uncomfortable levels.In contrast, the Control Group had fewer comfortable participants, with only 12% very comfortable and 28% comfortable.A greater proportion of the Control Group experienced discomfort, with 32% uncomfortable and 20% extremely uncomfortable.Overall, the Study Group demonstrated better intraoperative comfort compared to the Control Group.Conclusion-While CCLAD system is superior to traditional syringes in terms of physiological comfort, pain and anesthetic efficiency, its phycological deterrent.The study concludes that CCLAD is a highly effective tool for pain free dentistry, but further refinement in the ergonomics and size of hardware is necessary to mitigate patient anxiety.

Facility layout planning (FLP) in the agri-food sector faces unique complexities due to product perishability, biosafety regulations, and Industry 5.0 (I5.0) requirements. The reviewed literature is skewed toward static formulations that overlook detailed layout, demand uncertainty, and social sustainability. In response, a targeted review, reported following PRISMA 2020, and expert judgement yielded an ontological classification of ten characteristics influencing detailed agri-food layouts, whose relevance and relationships were supported by five external experts (S-CVI/Ave = 0.96); the system roles proposed by the authors were not reproduced in a blind assignment and remain modelling hypotheses. We then develop an eight-pillar conceptual framework addressing dynamic multi-period planning, stochastic uncertainty, multi-objective optimisation, comprehensive sustainability, human-centric ergonomics, operation-level routing, a bottom-up approach, and perishability as an endogenous variable. A diagnostic case study of an agri-food small and medium-sized enterprise (SME) illustrates how the classification structures the diagnosis of layout inefficiencies, such as products reaching customers with reduced shelf life. Aligned with I5.0 principles, this research provides a conceptual basis for models that treat perishability and human well-being as core design variables. The classification applies mainly to agri-food SMEs operating under make-to-order and just-in-time strategies; large make-to-stock manufacturers should also consider product homogeneity and storage-based product types.

This study aimed to evaluate undergraduate medical students’ awareness, use, perceived competence, and educational expectations regarding artificial intelligence (AI), three-dimensional portable document format (3D PDF), and deep learning in anatomy education. Data from 607 valid questionnaire responses were analyzed using descriptive statistics and chi-square tests of independence. Awareness of AI tools was high, with ChatGPT being the most recognized platform, followed by Gemini and OpenAI. Students mainly used AI to acquire theoretical knowledge, and AI use during studying anatomy ( p = 0.012). The frequency of AI use also varied according to both gender ( p = 0.028) and grade ( p = 0.010). Students reported a need for support in technical use, reliability checks, and ethical principles. Self-rated AI competence was generally moderate and differed significantly by gender ( p < 0.001). Deep learning was less familiar than AI and 3D PDFs. The use of 3D PDFs differed significantly by gender ( p = 0.025) and grade ( p = 0.028). Students considered 3D PDFs most applicable to anatomy education, followed by medical imaging and surgical planning ( p < 0.001). Overall, the findings indicate high digital awareness among medical students but limited structured preparation for responsible AI use, deep learning literacy, and visualization-based anatomical learning. Not applicable.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT This article examines a document that the ChatGPT interface made available during an exchange about capacity for saved memories. The response presented the reorganisation of writing rules for a narrative project as already completed, although my request concerned capacity alone, and no recorded prompt requested a file or specified the proposed hierarchy. Earlier, I had copied every visible saved memory entry verbatim into another document, allowing comparison in both directions to identify corresponding formulations and changes in their placement or prescriptive force. The phenomenological account follows my remembered reading and remains separate from those findings. In the linked document, rules appeared within a hierarchy not specified in my request and reading those formulations in their new positions changed how I understood decisions. Available records establish the limited request and the sequence through which the organised file became available without identifying the operations that produced the file. In this case, I formulated the rules without articulating their comprehensive relations, and recognising my formulations did not mean understanding what their new placement asserted. ChatGPT presented the organisation as already complete, whereas a human collaborator could have presented the same arrangement together with reasons.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: RESUMO: O excesso de estímulos comunicacionais no ambiente industrial tem gerado o fenômeno da fadiga de informação, comprometendo a retenção de orientações vitais de Segurança e Saúde Ocupacional (SSO). Este artigo investiga os impactos do ruído comunicacional na percepção de risco dos trabalhadores operacionais e propõe estratégias de simplificação e dinamização das mensagens corporativas. Por meio de uma pesquisa bibliográfico-qualitativa, analisa-se a aplicação do microlearning, do design de informação e do Diálogo Diário de Segurança (DDS) interativo como alternativas ao modelo tradicional de sobrecarga informativa. Conclui-se que a objetividade, a clareza visual e a interatividade são fundamentais para romper a dessensibilização dos colaboradores, garantindo que os alertas de risco sejam devidamente assimilados e colocados em prática. ABSTRACT: The excess of communication stimuli in the industrial environment has generated the phenomenon of information fatigue, compromising the retention of vital Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) guidelines. This article investigates the impacts of communication noise on operational workers' risk perception and proposes strategies for simplifying and streamlining corporate messages. Through qualitative-bibliographic research, the application of microlearning, information design, and interactive Daily Safety Dialogues (DDS) is analyzed as alternatives to the traditional model of information overload. It concludes that objectivity, visual clarity, and interactivity are essential to break through employee desensitization, ensuring that risk alerts are properly assimilated and put into practice.

Background and aims Employment opportunities for young adults with special education needs (YA-SEN) are often less favourable compared to their peers without SEN. They are often anxious during interviews, especially when answering open-ended questions with unfamiliar interviewers and unexpected interruptions occur. To fill the gap, we developed an interactive job interview training (JIT) system featuring a cat-shaped robot – JIT-bot.Sample JIT-bot was designed to provide an engaging, adaptive, and personalised training experience that supported users to practice and refine their interviewing skills in a less stressful environment. We recruited 28 participants in our study.Methods A mixed-method approach was employed, including proficiency tests, interviews, and questionnaires.Results Results provided preliminary evidence that the experimental group showed a statistically significant improvement in intrinsic motivation. In contrast, the behavioural engagement of the control group decreased slightly. These findings and feedback will suggest future enhancements to JIT-bot’s features and functions, making it a valuable tool to support JIT for YA-SEN.
topics: Assistive Technology in Communication and Mobility

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have brought about pivotal changes in writing assessment, particularly through comparisons with human raters. Nevertheless, most current studies are limited to analyzes that compare a small number of models with human raters and focus primarily on overall score differences or inter-rater agreement. This quantitative study compares 17 cutting-edge LLMs on the same dataset, examining the models’ scoring consistency, proximity to the mean scores assigned by human raters, and structural similarity and clustering analyzes of scoring behaviours relative to those of humans, based on analytic sub-dimensions, using a multidimensional approach. To that end, the research analyzed literary essays written by 46 first-year students at upper-intermediate proficiency in the English Language and Literature department of a state university in Türkiye, based on Ernest Hemingway's short story ‘The Cat in the Rain,’ using an expert-validated six-dimensional analytic rubric. The findings reveal substantial variability at the level of analytic sub-dimensions among 17 LLMs despite their proximity to experts in terms of overall scores. Moreover, these models clustered according to their average dimension-score profiles, while some displayed closer alignment with human rater profiles. Finally, while different correlation values were identified for each analytic dimension, high consistency was noted between the two expert raters with respect to overall scoring.

Scientific computing at HPC facilities increasingly relies on database infrastructure across a growing range of workloads: vector search and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), structured analytics, and AI-driven knowledge discovery over community corpora spanning documentation, experimental datasets, simulation outputs, and literature collections. These corpora are inherently shared facility resources, serving researchers, facility support staff, and AI agents across projects and institutions. Yet the supporting infrastructure remains built per project: each team provisions, configures, and operates its own database instance, with no facility-level registry, no shared identity layer, and no uniform interface for discovering or accessing the databases hosted across the facility. Commercial cloud platforms have addressed analogous needs through managed Database-as-a-Service offerings (e.g., Amazon RDS, Snowflake, Pinecone). However, these solutions do not transfer cleanly to scientific computing: they rely on proprietary identity systems, cannot directly access facility filesystems, and incur substantial data egress costs. We are building the missing piece: a managed database platform that lives inside the HPC facility, developed and evaluated on ALCF Polaris. One federated sign-in (Globus) brings a researcher — or an AI agent acting on their behalf — to every database the facility hosts, through a web UI, a scriptable API, or the Model Context Protocol. Governance, catalog, and access control are handled once by the platform and inherited by every project by default. The central design choice is scaling, native to HPC. Each workload is decomposed into its resource-consuming stages, and each stage can be scaled independently across nodes. As one representative example, a vector-search workload scales GPU-based embedding generation and search-index serving independently across nodes, reaching 5,197 queries/sec on 8 nodes (4.3× single-node) on ALCF Polaris and still climbing at maximum tested concurrency. Governance adds modest overhead at single-user load and becomes negligible under concurrency. In an end-to-end RAG pipeline built on this workload, retrieval contributes under 2% of total latency — the bottleneck has moved entirely to LLM generation. The same decomposition pattern is designed to extend to other workload types as additional engine adapters are integrated. The talk presents what changes when scientific data services are native to the facility: who can use them, what AI agents become capable of, and how a single platform can replace per-project infrastructure across an entire lab. We will share the design tradeoffs, what the scaling numbers mean for facility capacity planning, and the next stage of the design — co-locating the database service with model-inference services and scaling both on demand against shared facility resources, planned for the coming year. We invite peer facilities to adopt the platform and collaborate with us on a unified, cross-facility scientific data service.

Building a correct, performant HPC simulation from a scientific idea demands scarce, largely implicit expertise in numerical methods and library APIs. AI agents can now draft such code, but a draft that looks right is not necessarily one that an engineer can trust. We take a research-software-engineering (RSE) view of a real fusion-energy problem: not whether AI can replace that expertise, but what an RSE must build around a multi-agent AI system (orchestration, verification gates, provenance, and guardrails) to make its output trustworthy. Using a multi-agent AI system, from a plain-language prompt, we generate a PETSc simulation of the tokamak Grad–Shafranov equilibrium for nuclear fusion energy. In this poster, we will present the PETSc multi-agent system and demonstrate its application on this problem. The system includes a mathematical modeling agent, a numerical analysis agent, and an HPC code generation and execution agent. Around them, there is a project-owned orchestration driver that records every artifact (model, discretization decision, generated source code, build / run logs) with full provenance, so that runs are reproducible, resumable, and auditable. There is also a verification harness that gates every result before it is accepted. From the prompt (“Grad–Shafranov equilibrium for magnetically confined plasma in a tokamak”), the mathematical modeling agent identified the governing equation and returned its strong and weak forms; the numerical analysis agent selected a nonlinear solver on a structured grid; and the HPC code generation and execution agent produced a compact PETSc program that discretizes the operator on a distributed array with a true Jacobian matrix, and embeds a method-of-manufactured-solutions check. We do not treat “it compiled and ran” as sufficient evidence of success: an MPI-parallel grid-refinement study confirms second-order convergence. Verification, not the model’s confidence, decides acceptance. The same pipeline then produced one parameterized solver for several real-machine-shaped equilibria. Each was verified against an exact analytic benchmark and cross-checked against an independent community code. We scaled from the toy anchor to trustworthy shaped cases without re-architecting the generated solver. Running the AI agents on a shared HPC machine took environment and dependency wrangling, working-directory-independent process spawning, and graceful degradation when optional components were absent. There are also guardrails: in one instructive failure, a hard-coded iteration cap in the built-in orchestrator mislabeled a genuinely successful multi-stage run as a failure. We diagnosed it and contributed the fix upstream. Human effort is not eliminated but relocated, from writing solver code to engineering the orchestration, verification, and guardrails that make an AI system’s output trustworthy and its failures legible. We report per-run decision-gate metrics: correctness (model identified, program compiled and ran, convergence order), efficiency (execution duration, LLM / tool calls), and where human effort went (as a lightweight, reusable way to evaluate an agentic workflow rather than merely admire its output). The contribution is a candid, verification-driven account of how a research software engineer can wrap multi-agent AI code generation so that it produces trustworthy HPC simulation code for a flagship fusion-energy problem, and of the guardrails needed when it does not. In future work, we will raise the simulation difficulty to nonlinear profiles, time-dependent and resistive magnetohydrodynamics, and three-dimensional tokamak plasma, to map where the system succeeds and where it breaks, and to design guardrails and human-in-the-loop checkpoints that keep engineers in control as problems get harder.

Organisations are using crisis exercises to train their crisis management staff. Few studies have examined intuitive decision-making during exercises, which manifests itself in the form of heuristics: cognitive shortcuts. Identifying these heuristics duringobservation of exercises is complex due to the lack of a methodology for considering heuristics during exercises. To overcome this problem, we propose a methodology for observing linguistic markers to identify heuristics during 32 crisis exercises at the French Alternative Energies and Atomic Energy Commission. This research has shown that our methodology provides a framework for identifying seven specific heuristics during crisis exercises. We conclude the article with the contributions of our methodology and prospects for further development.

The co-evolution of micro-frontend UIs and backend microservices in cloud-native environments is complicated by UI–API semantic drift, dynamic workloads, and safe-deployment constraints. A tripartite agentic AI framework is introduced that combines reinforcement-learning (RL) agents for adaptive runtime control, large-language-model (LLM) synthesizers for automated artifact generation, and policy-as-code governors for security and compliance enforcement. The co-evolution process is formulated as a drift-aware Markov decision process, while Kubernetes-native traffic shifting supports progressive rollout and rollback. KubeSim was used for offline policy training; the reported performance results were obtained from live AWS EKS, Google GKE, and Azure AKS clusters. Across five benchmarks, the framework achieved a mean resolution success rate of 91.4%, compared with 62.0% for rule-based control, 71.1% for a controlled zero-shot LLM baseline, and 79.0% for partial RL. The framework also reduced normalized mean time to recovery by 80%, normalized change failure rate by 75%, and CPU utilization by 30 percentage points, while attaining a 98% audit pass rate. Component-removal and counterfactual-return analyses indicate complementary contributions from adaptive control, artifact synthesis, and policy enforcement. These results support the effectiveness, scalability, and governability of the framework for cloud-native enterprise digital transformation.

This chapter investigates how artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping medical professionalism, drawing on paradox theory, particularly the automation-augmentation paradox, to analyse how medical work is being redefined. While the medical profession has historically been able to balance resistance and adaptation to external pressures, AI represents a qualitatively different challenge: it encroaches on core professional expertise, introduces new knowledge agents into clinical decision-making, and disrupts traditional power structures between doctors, patients, and clinical knowledge. This chapter discusses how current AI deployments predominantly augment medical judgement, especially in specialties such as radiology, cardiology, and neurology. Yet the trajectory of AI integration suggests an evolving interplay between augmentation and automation, requiring clinicians to strategically engage with technologies that both complement and potentially transform their expertise. A central focus is on how AI might help address longstanding cognitive and implicit biases in medical decision-making related to race, gender, age, disability, and socioeconomic status. Although AI offers opportunities to reduce inequities, it also risks replicating or amplifying them due to biased training data, design choices, and opaque algorithms. This chapter argues for a hybrid model of medical doctor-AI collaboration that leverages mutual learning, preserves professional responsibility, and embeds safeguards to mitigate bias.

documents.abstract: Conflicts of interest: No conflicts of interest Sources of funding: No funding obtained Background Low back pain is the leading cause of years lived with disability worldwide and consequently it is the most common condition treated by physiotherapists in an out-patient setting. Physiotherapists also have a role to play in preventing spinal pain by providing ergonomic education. Purpose of Study To compare spinal angles whilst conducting a seated typing task with a self-selected optimal posture. Methods Cross-sectional pilot study. Twenty asymptomatic participants (9 male, 11 female, aged 19 to 23 years) adopted their normal sitting working posture using a laptop to conduct a typing task; they were then asked to adopt what they considered to be their best sitting posture. Retroreflective markers were attached to: L4, ASIS, PSIS, T12, C7, tragus and canthus. Spinal (neck, thoracic, lumbar and pelvic) angles were established via digital photographs using a bespoke MATLAB programme (MathWorks). Statistical analysis (Wilcoxon signed ranks tests) was conducted to determine between condition differences. Results No statistically significant results were observed between conditions for pelvic angles (p>0.05), however statistically significant differences (p<0.05) were observed for lumbar, thoracic and neck angles. In all cases participants adopted more ‘upright’ optimal postures. Conclusion The results suggest that a self-selected optimal posture varies significantly with a computer working posture for lumbar, thoracic and neck angles. Whilst pelvic angles were not significantly different between conditions, descriptive analysis demonstrated a more flexed position for all angles during the working posture. Whilst an optimal posture remains debatable, these differences highlight the need to identify interventions to address differences between working and optimal postures.

This article examines the figure of the first lady as a gender technology and a form of communicational mediation in Brazilian politics, challenging the androcentric canon of Political Communication. Drawing on feminist epistemology, situated knowledges, and the concept of coloniality of gender, it explores how gendered regimes of visibility co-produce authority, legitimacy, and recognition. Through an analysis of the Instagram profiles of Rosângela “Janja” Lula da Silva and Michelle Bolsonaro, the study investigates the sociotechnical architectures that organize processes of validation, surveillance, and disciplining of bodies. It argues that the first lady operates as a symbolic infrastructure of the political system within platformized communication environments.

Teachers’ competencies in artificial intelligence (AI) constitute a fundamental element for achieving innovative and effective education aligned with the demands of the twenty-first century. This study aims to propose a comprehensive model of teachers’ AI competencies based on the UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers and the European Digital Competence Framework for Educators (DigCompEdu), while adapting them to suit the needs of teacher preparation programs in faculties of education. The study adopts a qualitative approach using focus groups with experts in curriculum and instruction as well as educational technology. The domains, standards, and indicators of both frameworks were analyzed and discussed in order to derive a practical and contextually relevant model. The study resulted in a proposed model comprising five main domains, 15 standards, and 48 performance indicators, covering cognitive, pedagogical, ethical, professional, and assessment dimensions. It also provides practical recommendations for developing teacher preparation and continuous professional development programs, with a focus on integrating artificial intelligence in a responsible and effective manner to support interactive and inclusive learning for students.

Artificial intelligence is frequently described as if increasing computational capability were equivalent to increasing intelligence. This article rejects that scalar assumption and repositions artificial systems within a broader account of Natural Human Learning. It synthesises the 2026 Benjamin et al. work on cCC*, agency, bounded choice, Socialwork*, AEIOUF and consciousing; the Benjamin-McLaughlin account of Applied Curiosity and Augmented Understanding; the Benjamin-Palmer development of W-ALL as an externalised, revisable learning field; and the Natural Learning triptych's account of embodied, pre-verbal and AI-age learning. The synthesis is named LUMO: a human-governed learning environment in which machine generation enlarges the field of chances without displacing human authorship of choices, changes, responsibility or meaning. The paper advances four connected claims. First, learning begins before artificial representation - and before language: natural processes, embodiment, neural dynamics, encounter and difference provide the "horse" before the computational "cart". Second, uniquely human active agency (AAA) is categorical rather than scalar: capability may increase, but agency is not made "super" by more computation. Third, cCC* (Curiosity → Chances → Choices → Changes) is operationalised through the sequential AEIOUF process, A → E → I → O → U → F, with Conative Situational Integration (CSI) maintaining continuity across transitions. Fourth, LUMO should be coupled to protected canonical infrastructure: LUMO supports porous exploration; LIMO, with PROTON guardrails, protects provenance, permissions, canonical state and authorised change. R1-R16 and the 96-facet R × AEIOUF address space provide a selective-context routing layer, while CQI and CGI distinguish inquiry from generative construction. In the age of AI, the binding criterion becomes the preservation of the learner's CAN before externally supplied COULD. The resulting architecture reframes AI as a contingent support to human Natural Learning rather than its model, endpoint or successor. Sixteen research propositions are specified for empirical evaluation.

Construction projects are socio-technical systems requiring shared Situation Awareness (SA) to manage uncertainty and change. This study proposes Situation Monitoring, Analysis, and Reporting Teams (SMART) as a human-centred framework for structuring shared SA in construction. A thematic literature review identified a gap in understanding SA as an ongoing socio-technical process. An exploratory pilot study in a simulated modular construction setting examines communication patterns across four reporting phases: no reporting, self-reporting, SMART reporting, and post-intervention. SMART reporting was associated with a shift from fragmented to more structured and task-oriented communication, alongside increased information sharing and task-related exchanges. These patterns indicate coordination and information exchange, not direct measures of SA. The study makes three contributions: (1) reconceptualizing SA as an organizational socio-technical process rather than an individual or technology-driven outcome; (2) introducing SMART as a mechanism linking monitoring, sensemaking, and reporting; and (3) providing exploratory evidence that structured reporting is associated with communication patterns linked to SA processes. The controlled pilot setting and use of proxy indicators bounds findings. Future research should test SMART in real-world scenarios and examine its integration with digital and AI-assisted tools.

Purpose Adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) across small-scale businesses remains uneven even with the growing pace of digital transformation. Large enterprises are rapidly integrating AI into their operations, while there is still a barrier to adoption within small-scale businesses. This study proposes and examines an exploratory computational readiness index (CRI) that brings together behavioral, organizational and environmental dimensions to understand the preparedness of small-scale businesses in adopting AI. This index is offered as a preliminary firm-level diagnostic rather than a fully validated measure. Design/methodology/approach A quantitative, multi-source design was used, combining primary survey data from small-scale businesses with secondary global data collected from international sources and informal conversations with additional small business owners, managers and employees who fell outside the formal survey sample. Survey instruments were used to capture behavioral, organizational and environmental factors influencing the decision to adopt AI. This was also complemented with secondary global data collected and combined to derive the readiness index. Appropriate statistical tests were conducted to examine relationships among key dimensions and the overall readiness index. Findings Organizational factors like employee skills, motivation and opportunities were most consistently linked with readiness across groups, followed by individuals’ behavioral factors. External factors such as infrastructure and environment appeared to have comparatively smaller influence. The results of the study have been used to develop a readiness index that is intended to indicate the extent to which a small-scale business may be prepared to adopt AI. Practical implications The CRI proposed in this study can become a practical tool for policymakers and leaders within small-scale businesses for readiness assessment, prioritizing capability building within the organization rather than focusing on infrastructure investments alone. Originality/value This study contributes to the literature by proposing a novel framework for assessing AI readiness in small-scale businesses, integrating human, organizational and environmental dimensions.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: The rapid adoption of large language models (LLMs) transformed the way users obtained travel recommendations and generated personalized travel plans. However, standardized methods for comparing AI-generated travel itineraries across heterogeneous providers remained limited. This study presented the design, implementation, and experimental evaluation of a web-based benchmarking framework for the standardized and automated comparison of AI-generated travel plans. The framework integrated standardized prompt generation, structured JSON response processing, field-level comparison, deterministic rule-based scoring, model ranking, and exportable benchmarking reports. It was evaluated across three travel-planning scenarios involving Prague, Rome, and Tokyo, with three independent benchmark executions attempted for each scenario, resulting in 27 provider-level requests. Eight executions produced complete three-provider comparisons; one Rome execution was incomplete because Microsoft Phi returned malformed JSON. Across the eight complete executions, Gemini achieved a mean structural-completeness score of 57.00/57 (SD = 0.00), ChatGPT achieved 47.38/57 (SD = 3.02), and Microsoft Phi achieved 34.63/57 (SD = 5.26), with the same rank ordering observed in all complete comparisons. Supplementary constraint-compliance analysis demonstrated that structural completeness did not necessarily imply full satisfaction of travel requirements. Sustainability-related outputs were additionally examined as a separate dimension. The results demonstrated consistent framework operation under the tested scenarios and repetitions while emphasizing the need to distinguish structural completeness from constraint compliance, factual accuracy, practical feasibility, and sustainability-related performance.

Abstract Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has emerged as a transformative technology in higher education, significantly influencing the way students learn, access information, complete academic tasks, and develop professional skills. Tools such as ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, and Canva AI have become increasingly popular among commerce students for assignments, presentations, exam preparation, and concept clarification. While these technologies offer opportunities for personalized and efficient learning, their growing use also raises concerns regarding academic integrity, ethical practices, critical thinking, and dependency on AI-generated content. This study aims to examine the adoption and responsible use of Generative AI tools among commerce students in higher education and to evaluate their contribution towards sustainable learning. The research adopts a descriptive and analytical research design using primary data collected through a structured questionnaire administered to commerce students. The study focuses on students' awareness of GenAI tools, frequency and purpose of usage, responsible AI practices, AI dependency, and the perceived impact of AI on academic productivity and sustainable learning outcomes. The study is expected to provide insights into how commerce students integrate Generative AI into their academic learning and whether they use these tools responsibly by verifying information, avoiding plagiarism, and using AI as a learning aid rather than a substitute for independent thinking. It also explores the relationship between AI adoption, ethical usage, and sustainable learning practices in the context of higher education. The findings of this research are expected to assist educators, higher education institutions, and policymakers in designing AI literacy initiatives, promoting responsible AI usage, and developing pedagogical practices aligned with the objectives of sustainable and inclusive education. The study contributes to the growing body of literature on Artificial Intelligence in commerce education by emphasizing the importance of balancing technological innovation with ethical responsibility and lifelong learning in higher education. Keywords: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), Responsible AI, Sustainable Learning, Commerce Students, Higher Education, AI Ethics, Academic Productivity, Digital Literacy.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly changing the way education is delivered, experienced, and managed. AI-powered tools such as intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning platforms, automated assessment systems, chatbots, and generative AI can provide personalized learning, immediate feedback, and support for teachers. Recent research generally indicates positive effects on student learning, although the results vary considerably according to the subject, educational level, duration of intervention, and way AI is used. This paper attempts to study the impact of AI on education
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Agriculture remains the backbone of the Indian economy, contributing significantly to food security, employment, and rural development. However, increasing climate variability, soil degradation, water scarcity, pest infestations, fragmented landholdings, and the growing demand for sustainable food production have created substantial challenges for conventional farming practices. The rapid advancement of Data Mining, Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), and Deep Learning (DL) technologies has transformed precision agriculture by enabling intelligent analysis of large-scale agricultural data and supporting evidence-based decision-making. This systematic review critically examines recent developments in Data Mining frameworks and AI-enabled neural network technologies for environmentally sustainable Indian agriculture. The review synthesizes contemporary research on data acquisition, preprocessing, feature engineering, classification, clustering, association rule mining, regression analysis, and predictive analytics, together with advanced neural network architectures such as Artificial Neural Networks (ANN), Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Gated Recurrent Units (GRU), Transformer models, and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) [2], [3], [15], [18], [20], [21], [22], [43]. Furthermore, it evaluates their applications in crop yield prediction, soil health monitoring, intelligent irrigation, crop disease detection, weather forecasting, precision nutrient management, climate-resilient farming, and environmental sustainability [5], [11], [16], [24], [30], [36], [37]. The review identifies current research trends, methodological limitations, implementation challenges, and emerging opportunities while highlighting the need for scalable, interpretable, and resourceefficient intelligent agricultural systems tailored to India's diverse agro-climatic conditions. Finally, future research directions are proposed, emphasizing hybrid AI frameworks, Explainable AI, Edge Intelligence, Federated Learning, multimodal data integration, and sustainable decision-support systems. The findings provide a comprehensive knowledge base for researchers, policymakers, and agricultural practitioners seeking to develop intelligent, environmentally responsible, and sustainable agricultural ecosystems.

topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Air traffic control (ATC) simulators are essential tools for controller training, operational research and higher education, enabling realistic practice without affecting live air traffic. Although commercial simulation platforms are widely available, limited research has addressed structured engineering methodologies for designing university-based ATC simulation facilities that integrate regulatory, ergonomic, and technical requirements. This paper proposes a systems engineering framework for the conceptual design of university ATC simulators, combining stakeholder requirements, international aviation regulations, human factors principles, and engineering design within a requirement-driven workflow. The framework supports the design process from requirements analysis and functional decomposition to architectural layout, visualization system design, and technical infrastructure planning. Its applicability is demonstrated through the conceptual development of a 360° panoramic ATC simulator for higher education, comprising a 6.90 m diameter cylindrical screen driven by eight synchronized 4K laser projectors (effective horizontal resolution 19,968 pixels, 1.08 arcmin/pixel), a total usable floor area of approximately 278 m2, and an estimated installed electrical power of 25 kW. Furthermore, the framework incorporates universal design principles and specialized accessibility guidelines to ensure full ergonomic and physical accommodation for students with special needs. The proposed solution integrates the main functional areas of the simulation facility, including visualization, operator workstations, communication systems, and supporting infrastructure, while ensuring compliance with relevant standards and educational requirements. The proposed framework provides a structured and reusable methodology for the development of university ATC simulators and can support future educational and research simulation projects by improving design consistency, traceability, and scalability.

BACKGROUND: The growing application of artificial intelligence in dentistry has opened new opportunities for predicting peri-implantitis (PI) using convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Transfer learning, where knowledge from a model pre-trained on a large dataset is adapted to a new, domain-specific task, may enhance performance, particularly when medical datasets are limited. This study evaluated the ability of several pre-trained CNN architectures applied to baseline 2D intraoral radiographs to predict peri-implantitis onset. METHODS: A retrospective multi-center study was conducted at the University of Michigan and King's College London. A total of 195 implants (146 from Michigan and 49 from London) placed in 108 maintained patients were included. For each implant, a baseline periapical radiograph taken up to one year after prosthetic restoration was analyzed. Five pre-trained CNN architectures (ResNet50, DenseNet, VGG16, InceptionV3, EfficientNet) were combined with four transfer learning strategies: feature extraction (hybrid and non-hybrid), partial fine-tuning (50% of layers), and full fine-tuning. Models were trained using patient-wise splits to avoid leakage, and performance was evaluated on an independent test set using accuracy, area under the ROC curve (AUC), sensitivity, and specificity. RESULTS: All CNN architectures showed variable performance across transfer learning strategies. The non-hybrid feature extraction approach provided the most consistent discrimination, with the best models achieving AUC values between 0.74 and 0.83. InceptionV3 reached the highest AUC (0.83). Fine-tuning strategies yielded modest or low performance, with AUCs generally ranging from 0.42 to 0.69 across architectures. CONCLUSION: Non-hybrid feature extraction applied to pre-trained CNNs showed the most promising, though moderate, performance for predicting PI onset from baseline intraoral radiographs. These findings indicate that transfer learning may assist early risk stratification in implant dentistry, but larger prospective studies are needed before clinical adoption. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Deep learning models may serve as adjunctive tools to identify implants at higher risk for future PI based on routine baseline radiographs, supporting more individualized maintenance protocols and earlier preventive interventions.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: Crowds are increasingly invited to tackle complex innovation problems. However, our understanding of how crowds solve these problems has limited our ability to utilize them effectively. In this article, we examine how a crowd tasked with finding ways to preserve New Zealand’s native flora and fauna achieves solutions to this complex innovation problem through discussion. Our analysis reveals that discussions leading to innovative solutions differ from those leading to non-innovative solutions: innovation-yielding discussions (1) mobilize more Resources than Constraints, (2) converge on a single Goal, and (3) specify few (often one) responsible Subject(s); vis-à-vis, discussions leading to non-innovative solutions often surfaced multiple goals—thereby sustaining multiple problem framings—while subjects remained vague, implicit, or multiplied, and constraints frequently outnumbered resources. Moreover, we show how the specific weavings of these discursive elements support the crowd’s navigation of the complex innovation problem. Three discursive maneuvers – subject-goal anchoring, repurposing distant knowledge, and layering resources – are fundamental navigational tools used by the crowd to form what we call ‘action-oriented narratives:’ simple, dynamic, and evolving linguistic structures that enable collective problem exploration while giving room for localized improvisation. We contribute to the literature on problem solving by showing how specific linguistic activities alter individuals’ capacity to contribute to and solve complex problems. We also contribute to the literature on linguistic structures supporting innovation by showing that the types of discussions that support innovation depend on the openness of the setting.

Automatic crack segmentation in open-pit mining is constrained by the scarcity of representative, labeled datasets. Vision foundation models (VFMs) offer transferable visual representations, but their training-free performance on mining imagery and the benefits of synthetic-only adaptation remain insufficiently established. This study evaluates training-free VFM pipelines and investigates whether synthetic supervision improves their transfer to real-world crack imagery. SynthMineCrack is introduced as a diverse open-pit mining crack dataset, supporting model training and hyperparameter selection without real imagery or manual annotations. SAM 3 is adapted using low-rank adaptation (LoRA), layer normalization (LN) tuning, and adapters, individually and jointly, and compared with task-specific models trained on the same synthetic data. Evaluation on both in- and out-of-domain datasets shows that SAM 3 achieves the strongest training-free performance, while joint adaptation of all three operators improves intersection-over-union (IoU) on the mining evaluation dataset by 18.25 percentage points (pp). This configuration achieves a mean IoU of 69.39% across the five datasets, exceeding SegFormer, the strongest task-specific model, by 10.77 pp. Diagnostic analyses associate these gains with more complete crack recovery while the pretrained visual representation remains largely preserved. This configuration updates only 0.326% of the instantiated model’s parameter count and incurs little additional inference overhead. Together, these findings support synthetic-only adaptation as a practical means of improving SAM 3 for real-world crack segmentation while retaining inference requirements close to those of the base model.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing various sectors of society, and education is at the forefront of this transformation. These emerging technologies are reshaping how students interact with content and how teachers design instruction, which create an urgent need for innovation. The success of such innovation in schools often depends on leadership that is flexible and adaptive to diverse cultural, technological, and organizational contexts. Drawing on the case of Hong Kong, this study investigated how school leaders perceive educational innovation in an AI-driven era and how they enact their leadership to engage teachers in these initiatives. Findings show that leaders recognize the multifaceted challenges of AI integration and use adaptive leadership to address them by prioritizing adaptive challenges, mobilizing teachers, and empowering them to experiment and change. The study contributes empirical evidence on adaptive leadership in AI-driven education and recommends practical strategies for engaging teachers in innovation. Its implications extend beyond Hong Kong and provide valuable guidance for school systems worldwide as they navigate ongoing innovation and build the capacity to meet future challenges.

BACKGROUND: Despite growing interest in artificial intelligence (AI) in health professions education, qualitative evidence for integarting AI-supported instructional redesign on teaching practices and students' experiences in undergraduate dental education remains limited. The aim of this study was to explore the educational impact of AI-supported instructional redesign of lessons in undergraduate dental education. METHODS: We conducted this inductive qualitative thematic analysis in an undergraduate dental education setting. Existing lessons were redesigned using AI-supported recommendations to strengthen alignment between learning objectives, authentic clinical contexts, and expected clinical outcomes. Data were collected through classroom observations and students' focus group discussions. An inductive thematic analysis was performed, and findings from multiple data sources were curated, collecetd, and triangulated to enhance credibility. RESULTS: AI-supported instructional redesign transformed teaching by promoting authentic clinical scenarios, clinically oriented discussions, and explicit reasoning activities. Thematic analysis identified four interconnected themes: (1) a shift from teacher-centred knowledge delivery to facilitation of clinical reasoning; (2) transformation from passive attendance to active cognitive engagement; (3) building clinical meaning through authentic clinical contexts and collaborative dialogue; and (4) creating conditions for professional learning through psychological safety. AI functioned as a pedagogical design-support tool rather than replacing the educators' instructional role. Overall, the observed educational changes appeared to arise primarily from the pedagogical redesign enabled by AI-supported planning rather than from students' direct interaction with AI. CONCLUSION: This study endorses the role of AI-supported instructional redesign in enriching the existing undergraduate dental curriculum. This approach can potentially help educators align learning objectives, instructional strategies, and authentic clinical contexts. The reported educational modifications reflect primarily the implementation of learner-centred and clinically oriented pedagogical strategies, with AI functioning as a design-support mechanism rather than as a direct instructional agent.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Ground-level air quality affects human health, well-being, and social outcomes. Gold-standard monitoring relies on calibrated, ground-based sensors that can be costly to install and maintain, limiting spatial coverage especially in resource-constrained regions that face higher pollution burdens. Recent advances in satellite remote sensing and machine learning offer a pathway to address these limitations by extending the spatial and temporal coverage of monitoring networks. However, models trained at national or global scales often exhibit substantial variability in regional performance, particularly in environments that are data-sparse or with heterogeneous emission sources. In this work, we investigate the benefits of developing a regional model for the American Gulf South. We develop an ensemble machine learning model that integrates satellite-derived NO2 retrievals with auxiliary data sets, including pretrained AlphaEarth location embeddings, to incorporate globally learned spatial representations into a regional framework. We show that these embeddings improve model performance and enable the most detailed estimates to date: ∼1 km × 1 km estimates of daily maximum NO2 across the Gulf South. These results demonstrate how combining regional modeling approaches with global foundation model representations can improve air quality estimation in complex environments, providing new information to support exposure assessment and decision-making in under-monitored communities.

While autoregressive foundation models trained on limit order book (LOB) data show state-of-the-art performance for market simulation, pre-training with cross-entropy neither penalizes the compounding of sampling errors over free-running rollouts nor targets desired market properties. We introduce a post-training method for LOB foundation models using a Wasserstein generative adversarial network (GAN) objective. A critic, trained online on rollouts through the true, non-differentiable matching engine, guides updates from evolution strategies over rank-4 LoRA perturbations of the pre-trained generator, under a KL trust region. For efficiency, we use EGGROLL (Evolution Guided GeneRal Optimisation via Low-rank Learning), a memory-efficient variant of evolution strategies. On a held-out panel, adversarial post-training improves LOB-Bench realism by 17.6% (WS-21) and 17.0% (Mean-$L_1$), while selection-matched random-perturbation and compute-matched continued-pre-training controls yield no improvement. Post-training is thus a necessary stage that more pre-training does not replace. Per-position divergence measurements show that it slows error accumulation over 500-message rollouts from $3.1\times$ to $2.3\times$. Adversarial post-training is also inexpensive, requiring under 50M training tokens and 12 GPU-hours per seed, three orders of magnitude below the 48B-token pre-training budget. Ablations over critic inputs, optimizers, and the population-rollout trade-off, together with an analysis of reward hacking, yield practical design guidelines for adversarial post-training.

With the widespread adoption of large language models (LLMs) across languages and domains, AI safety has emerged as a critical global concern. However, due to resource constraints, research and development efforts tend to prioritize a limited number of high-resource languages, leaving many others, especially those spoken in Africa, underrepresented. While existing research on language "resource-ness" has largely examined whether sufficient resources are available to develop language technologies, the question of whether languages are adequately represented in AI safety research has received attention only more recently. This report examines the readiness of African languages for inclusion in AI safety discussions, drawing on existing literature and data. It considers four factors: the availability of AI-relevant resources, including text data; national AI policy support; performance on established text benchmarks; and speaker population. Based on these factors, languages are grouped into four readiness categories: fully ready, mostly ready, emerging, and foundational support needed. This classification is intended to inform the inclusion of African languages in AI safety benchmarks, highlight varying levels of preparedness, and guide strategic investment in data development, policy, and community engagement for underrepresented languages.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) designed to interact with users are typically trained to respond appropriately to harmful or toxic content. However, ensuring appropriate responses becomes more challenging in diverse linguistic and cultural contexts, where safety risks may be expressed or interpreted differently. Building safe AI systems therefore requires detecting safety risks, understanding their nature, and responding appropriately, while accounting for linguistic and cultural variations that add complexity to each stage. In this work, we introduce AfriGuard, a culturally grounded multilingual dataset for studying harmful intent, safety-category understanding, and refusal behavior across 10 African languages and English. Our findings reveal that guardrail models underperform both open- and closed-source LLMs on safety-intent and safety-category classification, while models show limited understanding of appropriate safety behavior, scoring below 60% F1. We further find that models often fail to respond appropriately to unsafe prompts not because they explicitly refuse, but because they produce linguistically inadequate responses that result in incidental non-assistance rather than proper refusals. Finally, using AfriGuard, we develop efficient guardrail models that achieve performance competitive with models up to 30x larger, introduce refusal detectors that improve average performance by 43.9% over existing detectors, and demonstrate that supervised fine-tuning can substantially improve overall safety performance.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Agent-friendly Provenance Capture with con-duct Presenters Austin Macdonald , ORCID 0000-0002-8124-807X Cody C. Baker , ORCID 0000-0002-0829-4790 John A. Lee , ORCID 0000-0001-5884-4247 Yaroslav O. Halchenko , ORCID 0000-0003-3456-2493 All: Center for Open Neuroscience, Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences, Dartmouth College Keywords agentic workflows, provenance, reproducibility, resource monitoring, HPC Abstract Whether trying out a new tool, testing pipelines, or meticulously analyzing data for research, the daily work of RSEs and their agents depends on keeping context lean but relevant. The terminal outputs of tools and scripts frequently hold the necessary information, but they are often either bloating an agent’s context window, or forgotten after a human’s terminal scrolls past the buffer. con-duct is a lightweight, Python-based command line tool with no third-party dependencies: just use duct instead of to run a command. A wrapped run leaves a trail: full stdout and stderr streamed to disk (or skipped, for sensitive output); resource usage sampled across the command’s process tree; and a record of the invocation, wall clock time, peak memory, exit code, and system and environment details. Workflow managers and experiment trackers produce richer records (the poster compares them); con-duct collects basic provenance with so little effort it can be used on everything, producing uniform records. In daily work, humans and agents now execute commands side by side. Using con-duct, the full record stays out of the context window until it is needed. Even better, multiple runs can be filtered and grepped, ready for the questions nobody knew to ask. When did our tests start having that warning? Did this run take longer? con-duct ls makes the answers discoverable, filtering on any captured field with a Python expression: con-duct ls -e "message==' '" retrieves runs tagged at capture time with duct -m " ". con-duct ls -e "exit_code != 0" lists failures. con-duct ls -e "peak_rss > 8e9" finds runs that exceeded a memory budget. At the tool level, projects can adopt con-duct internally rather than reinventing per-tool monitoring: ReproNim’s containers [5] and ReproStim [6] both offer it already, and the same con-duct ls queries read their records. For research, the record stops being a convenience, and starts being a part of the provenance chain [4]. Pairing con-duct with datalad (git-based version control for data)[2] is an easy win for rigor. datalad run "duct ..." completes the execution and then commits the diff (including the duct logs). On HPC, last month’s measured wall time and peak memory are already recorded, and can help inform tomorrow’s SLURM request. When an expensive job fails, the bug-report evidence is already on disk, no re-run necessary to file an issue. con-duct is on PyPI (pip install con-duct), conda-forge, registered as RRID:SCR_025436, and developed openly [1]. The poster shows three real cases: an fMRIPrep run on a SLURM cluster, its five hours of CPU and memory plotted from the record; a Kubernetes upgrade worked deploy by deploy, with every attempt’s command, exit code, and wall time kept by con-duct; and duct wrapped around duct to measure its own overhead. Keeping agents’ work auditable will take more than one tool; con-duct is one small piece: a wrapper that makes the agent’s work, like the human’s, leave a trace. Acknowledgments We thank the broader ReproNim and OpenNeuro communities for ongoing feedback on con-duct’s design and use. con-duct’s resource-monitoring approach is based on brainlife’s smon [3]. AI disclosure (per IEEE policy): Prose in the Abstract and Connection-to-Mission sections was drafted with assistance from Anthropic’s Claude; the authors specified the content, edited the text, and verified all technical claims, commands, and references. The con-duct software itself is developed with AI assistance, and with human review of all merged code. References con-duct. Center for Open Neuroscience. https://github.com/con/duct. RRID:SCR_018467. The dev-side payoff (reaching back into outputs that would otherwise be gone) was an unexpected bonus. As LLM agents take on more of the executing (writing throwaway pipelines, exploring datasets, calling tools), the volume of unrecorded work explodes: more commands, more parallel streams, results produced faster than anyone reads them. RSEs are the people who decide whether that work remains auditable: who preserve the context, make it discoverable, and keep capture cheap enough that nobody skips the step. Integrating at the tool level saves each project from building its own monitoring and logging, and keeps the records uniform across tools, so the collection stays queryable as a whole.

Diagnosing production incidents is still largely manual: on-call engineers gather logs, errors and deployment history from separate tools before they can reason about a cause. Large language models (LLMs) can suggest root causes, but a model that sees only an incident summary lacks evidence, and an unchecked suggestion can mislead. This paper aims to give an LLM agent the evidence it needs while keeping a human in control. We present Phase 1 of an open, four-module platform: a non-blocking Java SDK that captures exceptions, latency and deployments; a multi-tenant Spring Boot backend that groups repeated errors into incidents by stack hash; a FastAPI service in which a tool-calling LLM investigates each incident only through audited APIs; and a dashboard where an operator approves or rejects every suggestion. We evaluate it by injecting seven kinds of real faults into an instrumented service. All 21 trials were detected, with mean detection times of 8–12 s for exception faults and 25–45 s for resource faults, and no incident was raised in 8 min of fault-free operation. The SDK added a median of 14 µs per captured error and stayed non-blocking when the backend was down. A successful investigation used about 11k–24k tokens and two to three minutes; of five graded suggestions, two were correct, two partly correct and one wrong despite a confidence of 0.78. The results show that telemetry-grounded investigation is practical for small teams, and that self-reported confidence must not replace human review.

Abstract In mechanics of materials, many powerful methods are accessible only to experts. Constitutive models, for example, describe the relation between stress and strain in materials and are a core ingredient of simulations from structural engineering to biomechanics. Yet building and using such models requires specialized expertise—a barrier for the many potential users trained in other fields. Artificial intelligence based on foundation models, increasingly organized as agents, is beginning to lower this barrier by allowing users to generate tailored models on demand. The same development is underway in many other fields where specialized tools have long been hand‐crafted anew for each task. We call this emerging paradigm the on‐the‐fly generation of physical models : from a plain request, an agent creates a physical model on demand—from scratch and tailored to the problem. Its appeal is accessibility and flexibility. As a consequence, the lasting artifact is no longer a fixed model but the orchestration and prompting of the agents that produce it. This review surveys the concepts behind the paradigm, within mechanics of materials and in neighboring fields, and examines them through two lenses: effectiveness (the accuracy of the generated models) and trustworthiness (their physical admissibility). Trustworthiness is pursued along two routes: deepening the agent's integration under explicit validation, or restraining its autonomy in favor of trusted components. Given the rapid progress of foundation models, and the bitter lesson that general methods leveraging computation tend to prevail, we call for paradigms designed to scale with this progress rather than to compete with it.

This paper mainly deals with the second order nonlinear difference equations with advanced argument where and is a ratio of odd positive integers. This paper presents an AI-based framework for the prediction and classification of oscillatory behavior in nonlinear discrete-time dynamical systems. The proposed approach employs artificial intelligence and machine learning techniques to analyze the dynamic behavior of nonlinear discrete-time systems and identify oscillatory and non-oscillatory solution patterns. Relevant system parameters and solution characteristics are extracted and used to develop predictive models capable of classifying the long-term behavior of system trajectories. The proposed framework provides an efficient data-driven approach for detecting oscillations and predicting the qualitative behavior of nonlinear discrete-time dynamical systems. Numerical experiments and illustrative examples are presented to validate the effectiveness and accuracy of the proposed AI-based prediction and classification methodology.
topics: Advanced Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems

documents.abstract: On October 19th, 2026, a post on Substack https://open.substack.com/pub/generativevalue/p/what-has-to-go-right-to-justify-the?utm_source=share&utm_medium=android&r=3nsea2 asked a question that the AI industry has not answered: "What has to go right to justify thetrillions being spent on AI CapEx?" The post models $1.5 trillion in CapEx for 2027. It estimates the revenue threshold at $600 billion by late 2027 and $1.1 trillion by 2028. It names three conditions: the frontier keeps getting better at high-value work, AI diffuses through the economy, and value doesn't get whittled away by competition. The post is correct about the question. It is incomplete about the answer. This paper argues that the post names the cost of the stochastic architecture, but does not name the alternative architecture — one that requires almost no CapEx at all. The paper makes four claims: First: The stochastic path requires $1.5 trillion in CapEx. It cannot be certified under anyfunctional safety standard. It produces the four walls: CapEx, hallucination, energy, water, and AlCapone-LLM. Second: The deterministic path requires $2.1M–$6.5M for the first deployment. It can be certified under ISO 26262, IEC 61508, DO-178C, and IEC 62443. It runs on a $12microcontroller. Third: The ratio is roughly 1:500,000. The two paths are not competing on the same economics. Fourth: The 4 norms are the certification path. The deterministic architecture passes them byconstruction. The stochastic architecture cannot pass them at all. The paper does not argue that creativity needs scaling. It argues that creativity is selection.Selection requires a criterion. A criterion is not a scale. It is a discovery. The corpus has 300+papers to prove it.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are rapidly evolving from experimental tools into integral components of clinical care. In diagnostics, treatment planning, and operational management, AI systems can augment clinicians&s; capabilities, enable earlier and more accurate interventions, and improve the patient experience—particularly for those seeking care across international borders. However, they also raise important questions about data privacy, algorithmic bias, transparency, and accountability. International organisations, notably the World Health Organization (WHO), now emphasise that AI in healthcare must be guided by robust ethical standards and tailored to the realities of diverse healthcare systems, including those that serve large numbers of medical tourists. This chapter examines how AI is being deployed throughout the medical tourism pathway—from early diagnosis and pre-travel screening to in-hospital decision support and post-travel follow-up—featuring real-world clinical examples and case studies from Apollo Hospitals in India and the Mayo Clinic in the United States. It also addresses the conditions under which AI can genuinely humanise, rather than dehumanise, globally mobile healthcare.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming the media ecosystem by changing how information is gathered, verified, produced, personalized, distributed and monetized. News organisations can use AI for transcription, translation, data analysis, recommendation, automated production, audience analytics, fact-checking support, visualisation and the creation of new formats. At the same time, AI introduces significant risks concerning misinformation, deepfakes, algorithmic bias, privacy, intellectual property, opacity, labour displacement, editorial accountability and the erosion of public trust. These tensions are particularly important in India, where the media environment is linguistically diverse, mobile-first, platform-dependent and characterised by a rapid expansion of digital and creator-led news. This conceptual paper examines the challenges, prospects and opportunities created by AI for Indian media and develops an integrated framework for responsible AI-enabled journalism. Drawing on stakeholder theory, the resource-based view, institutional theory, diffusion of innovations and the emerging literature on algorithmic and automated journalism, the paper conceptualises AI capability as an enabling resource whose value depends on editorial governance, human oversight, professional competence, data quality and regulatory conditions. The framework proposes that AI adoption influences media performance through a mediating mechanism of newsroom capability and workflow transformation, while ethical governance, organisational readiness and regulatory clarity moderate the relationship. The paper argues that AI should be treated neither as a substitute for journalism nor simply as a productivity tool, but as a socio-technical capability that must remain accountable to journalistic values. For Indian media, the most promising opportunities lie in multilingual journalism, accessibility, local and hyperlocal coverage, data-driven reporting, personalised public-interest information, newsroom efficiency and new digital business models. However, these opportunities can be realised only when media organisations establish transparent AI-use policies, verification protocols, disclosure standards, staff training, data safeguards and mechanisms for human editorial responsibility. The paper concludes with implications for media managers, journalists, educators, regulators and technology providers, and proposes directions for future empirical research.

Coding agents like Claude Code and GitHub Copilot have significant implications for the way software is built and maintained in the sciences. Some of these implications center around changes in practice, such as greater or worse productivity and the need for verification practices (He et al., 2025; O'Brien, 2025a; O’Brien, 2025b; Besser et al., 2026; O'Brien and Eisty, 2026). Another dimension of concern, however, is how research software development work will be reorganized around the presence of coding agents. Broader discourse has focused on the possibility of replacement or simple automation of software engineering work by agents, but, as with prior developments, the change is more likely to involve a more complex re-ordering of the work of producing software (Jarrahi, 2018; see also Gesing, 2025). Emerging work in industrial and open source contexts, for instance, suggests that coding agents can affect the interactions around code review (Song et al., 2024; Agarwal et al., 2026a), assume different roles in the development process (Agarwal et al., 2026b), and can change where particular kinds of development work fall in a team or community (Xu et al., 2025). This poster explores these shifts in the context of RSE work by examining dynamics of re-delegation going on around the adoption of coding agents by researchers and RSEs. Based on interviews with 25 RSEs and RSE managers in the US, we first outline these RSEs’ rationales about what makes research software development either amenable or unsuitable for the use of AI coding agents. These include niche codebases, siloed working environments, savvy end users, prevalence of prototyping, and the importance of problem formation. We then outline three dynamics of re-delegation, each of which represents a shift in the way work is divided up and assigned (or taken on) amongst human and non-human actors (Ribes et al., 2013). These are: enabling end-user development, delegating implementation, and taking on AI training roles. In some cases our interlocutors report quite different and sometimes contradictory experiences across these categories. This raises two questions that can help stimulate further discussion on this topic: 1) What aspects of RSE working environments might contribute to RSEs’ different experiences with AI coding agents? 2) What organizational changes could RSEs or RSE teams make that might mitigate some of the problems associated with the growing usage of AI coding agents while making best use of those agents’ benefits?
